title: Familiarity Mediated Competitive‐Signaling Networks in Female Brown‐Headed Cowbirds (Molothrus ater)
content:
Female brown-headed cowbirds used head-up displays as competitive signals, with display frequency positively associated with reproductive output. Although overall display rates did not differ between familiar and novel flocks, familiar females preferentially directed displays toward reproductively active females. These findings suggest that social familiarity may shape the targeting of competitive signals, potentially helping females direct interactions toward key rivals.


ABSTRACT

Social familiarity can shape how individuals interact within animal societies, yet its influence on female–female competition remains poorly understood. I investigated whether social familiarity alters the organization of competitive interactions among female Brown-headed Cowbirds (Molothrus ater) by comparing flocks composed of familiar individuals with flocks composed of previously unfamiliar individuals. Competitive interactions were quantified using head-up displays, a widespread agonistic signal in the Icteridae. Females that performed more head-up displays laid significantly more eggs, indicating that competitive signaling was associated with reproductive success. Although the overall frequency of head-up displays did not differ between familiar and novel flocks, familiarity altered the structure of competitive interactions. In familiar flocks, head-up displays were directed preferentially toward reproductively active females, whereas no such pattern emerged in novel flocks. These findings suggest that social familiarity improves the targeting of female competitive behavior by increasing social knowledge of potential rivals and highlight how familiar flock organization can structure competitive interactions within fission–fusion societies.
author: Gregory Kohn
